title: What is consistent hashing, how does it minimize data movement when adding/removing nodes (only K/N keys move instead of all), and what is a virtual node (multiple hash positions per physical node for better balance)?

s1_definition.oneliner: Consistent hashing moves only K/N keys when nodes change, and virtual nodes give each physical node many ring spots for even balance.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Hash ring** – both keys and nodes are mapped onto a fixed circular hash space; each key belongs to the first node found clockwise.
- **Minimal movement** – adding or removing a node moves only the keys in that node's arc, about K/N of all keys, instead of a near-total reshuffle.
- **Virtual nodes** – each physical node is hashed to many positions on the ring, smoothing out uneven arcs and allowing weighted assignment for heterogeneous hardware.
- **Modulo hashing problem** – `hash(key) % N` changes almost every assignment when N changes, making online scaling impractical.
- **Production use** – underpins Dynamo-style stores, Cassandra, Redis clusters, and distributed caches.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India placing all accounts around a clock face, and each shard sits at a spot on the clock. An account is handled by the next shard clockwise. If the bank opens a new shard, only the accounts in that one arc move: everyone else stays put. Virtual nodes are like giving each shard many spots around the clock so no single shard accidentally ends up with a giant arc.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Consistent Hash Ring with Virtual Nodes:

         0°
         │
    A#2 ─●── B#1
    /          \
  C#3            A#1
  │                │
  B#2            C#1
    \          /
    A#3 ─●── B#3
         │
        180°

  A, B, C = physical nodes
  A#1, A#2, A#3 = virtual nodes for A

  Key K hashed to 45° ──▶ next clockwise = A#1 ──▶ physical Node A

  Adding Node D:
  Insert D#1, D#2, D#3 at their hash positions
  Only keys in D's arcs move to D
  All other keys stay put
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Consistent hashing maps both keys and nodes onto a single circular hash space, and each key is owned by the first node found clockwise. The payoff is that adding or removing a node moves only the keys in that node's arc, about K/N of all keys, instead of the near-total reshuffle that modulo hashing causes when the node count changes.

A virtual node is one of many ring positions assigned to the same physical node. By giving each physical node 150 positions, its ownership is split into many small arcs that average out to an even share, preventing hotspots. Bigger machines can receive more virtual nodes for weighted assignment.

This is the technique behind Dynamo-style stores, Cassandra, and many distributed caches. It also gives replication for free by walking clockwise to the next few distinct physical nodes.

At the National Bank of India, Pankaj routes sharded accounts by account id on a consistent-hash ring with 150 virtual nodes per shard. Adding a shard relocates only the small fraction of accounts in the new shard's arcs rather than every account.

Remember one sentence: consistent hashing moves only K/N keys when nodes change, and virtual nodes give each physical node many ring spots for even balance.

---

keyPoints: Modulo hashing reshuffles nearly all keys when the node count changes, making online scaling impractical.
Consistent hashing maps keys and nodes onto a ring; adding a node moves only about K/N of all keys.
Virtual nodes assign many ring positions per physical node, smoothing out uneven load distribution.
Heterogeneous hardware can be weighted by assigning more virtual nodes to larger machines.
Replication is achieved by walking clockwise to the next N distinct physical nodes.
Use 100-200 virtual nodes per physical node and a good hash function like MurmurHash3.
Consistent hashing underpins Cassandra, Dynamo-style stores, Redis clusters, and distributed caches.
